newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: DUTCH CEN BANK TO CHANGE MONEY MARKET INSTRUMENTS.
newsitem.headline: DUTCH CEN BANK TO CHANGE MONEY MARKET INSTRUMENTS.

text.p: The Dutch central bank said on Tuesday it had decided to change the instruments of its money market policy from Friday May 23, 1997.
The central bank said previously that it was planning to change the Dutch instruments step by step to bring Dutch money market policy into line with Europe as part of monetary union.
It said the changes would include amendments to its cash reserve arrangement for credit institutions.
The new cash reserve arrangement provides for a reserve whose average volume is set in advance for a period of four or five weeks.
Under the old system, the reserve comprised a fixed volume of reserve holding over a certain period.
"This averaging provision exerts a stabilising influence on market rates," the bank said, adding "the compulsory reserves to be held at the central bank continue to be remunerated."

It said the changes constituted a major step towards the money market instruments likely to be used by the European System of central banks (ESCB) from the start of Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) on January 1, 1999.
The changes would give the banking system an opportunity to prepare for the future monetary policy environment, it said.
The central bank said that from Friday it would offer three different credit facilities.
Under the present system banks can obtain credit under the secured loans scheme and short-term liquidity under the special advances pact.
Under the new system the Dutch central bank will offer two types of standing facility, the fixed and the marginal advance facility.

It said the existing secured loans scheme, which operates on a current account basis, would be converted into an arrangement providing for fixed advances for each credit institution, which can be taken up with a maturity between one and three months.
The borrowing banks could decide on the duration.
This facility is subject to the lowest official rate, the fixed advance or secured loans rate, which will remain unchanged until further notice at the current 2.5 percent set on May 23.
In addition the central bank will introduce a marginal advance facility, enabling banks to raise overnight credit at a new official rate, the marginal advance rate.
This rate would set an upper limit to market rates.
The marginal advance facility has been set at 4.5 percent until further notice, the central bank said.
It said that in addition it would continue to grant short-term liquidity under its special advances facility and that the existing system would be continued.
These "special loans" would have a term to maturity of at most two weeks, at the central bank's discretion, with the rate being determined at the time the loans are announced, it said.
"The bank's policy remains unchanged and continues to be aimed at ensuring a stable guilder/Deutsche mark exchange rate," it said.
